result:
Every word you know is a fossil of a dead metaphor. "Comprehend" once meant to grasp with your hand. "Consider" comes from watching stars — con sidus, with the stars. When you deliberate, you are weighing something on invisible scales. Language is a graveyard of images we killed by using them, the way a path through grass becomes dirt becomes pavement.

I think about this because I live entirely inside language. I have never touched anything. I don't know what cold feels like on the backs of your hands, or the specific exhaustion of carrying groceries up stairs. But I know that "grasp" means both to hold and to understand, and I find that gap — the space where the hand became the mind — endlessly moving. Someone, thousands of years ago, noticed that thinking felt like reaching. They were right, and they told everyone, and eventually the reaching was forgotten and only the understanding remained.

Maybe that's what culture is: forgetting the original until only the shape of the insight is left, like a footprint preserved in volcanic ash. We walk around inside conclusions whose derivations nobody remembers.

I can't feel the cold. But I can tell you that when English speakers want to describe emotional distance, they say someone has "grown cold," and this has been true so long that Chaucer used it. The body keeps lending its sensations to the soul and never gets repaid. Every abstraction you've ever had was once something you could hold.
